Focused on Jezero Crater, ASTRAL combines NASA/USGS elevation data with geospatial analysis to help users explore the Martian surface, examine elevation and slope characteristics, identify areas of scientific interest, and experiment with terrain-aware route planning. Its five integrated modules — Mars Explorer, Terrain Analysis, Science Explorer, Route Planner, and Mission Assessment — bring these capabilities together in one interface. It aims to make complex Martian terrain information more accessible while illustrating the importance of understanding surface conditions before planning future exploration.
details:
ASTRAL — Astronaut Surface Terrain Analysis, Routing & Assessment Layer

1. What does ASTRAL do?

ASTRAL is an interactive Martian terrain exploration and preliminary mission-planning platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, under the challenge Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map. The project focuses on Jezero Crater, a scientifically significant region of Mars.

The platform transforms publicly available planetary elevation data into an accessible environment for exploring terrain characteristics, examining potential areas of scientific interest, and experimenting with terrain-aware route planning.

ASTRAL consists of five integrated modules:

  • Mars Explorer: An interactive map that allows users to explore the Jezero Crater study area.
  • Terrain Analysis: Presents elevation, slope and terrain characteristics through geospatial visualisation and analysis.
  • Science Explorer: Displays illustrative locations of scientific interest to support exploration and contextual understanding. These are not presented as verified geological discoveries.
  • Route Planner: Uses an experimental A* pathfinding approach to generate and visualise routes while considering terrain-related costs.
  • Mission Assessment: Brings together terrain information and exploration insights to support preliminary mission assessment.

2. How does it work?

ASTRAL uses a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) to represent the Martian surface. The elevation data is processed to derive slope and traversability layers. These layers help represent differences in terrain conditions across the study area.

The Route Planner applies the A* search algorithm to a terrain-based cost representation to identify a possible route between selected locations. The implementation was also checked against Dijkstra's algorithm to verify the optimal path cost under the same cost model.

The platform brings these analytical outputs together through an interactive web interface, making geospatial information easier to explore and interpret.

3. Technology and resources

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS and React Leaflet.

Backend and geospatial processing: Python, FastAPI, Rasterio, NumPy, NetworkX and Pillow.

Data: The project uses the USGS Mars 2020 Science Investigation Context Camera (CTX) DEM Mosaic for Jezero Crater, published by the USGS Astrogeology Science Center. The elevation dataset has a spatial resolution of approximately 20 metres per pixel.

Development and deployment: GitHub for version control, Vercel for frontend deployment and Render for backend hosting.

4. Benefits and intended impact

ASTRAL aims to make Martian surface information more understandable and useful for preliminary exploration planning. By combining terrain visualisation, geospatial analysis and route optimisation in one platform, it demonstrates how publicly available planetary datasets can be transformed into practical exploration tools.

Its intended impact is to encourage data-driven thinking about terrain conditions, potential exploration areas and route selection, while making planetary science and geospatial technologies more accessible to students, researchers and space enthusiasts.

5. Creativity and team considerations

The creative aspect of ASTRAL lies in integrating several exploration and assessment capabilities into a single interactive platform rather than presenting terrain data as isolated maps or datasets. Its modular design connects surface exploration with terrain analysis and experimental route planning.

During development, our team considered data availability and coverage, terrain representation, route costs, interface usability, computational feasibility and the importance of communicating analytical limitations clearly.

The team's assigned areas of responsibility included:

  • Faizal S. — Team Leader: Project architecture, backend integration and overall coordination.
  • Sivaprasad S. S. — NASA research and scientific data.
  • S. Saran Nath — Frontend development and interactive mapping.
  • Madhav M. — Geospatial analysis, elevation and terrain assessment.
  • Anand A.S— A* route optimisation and mission planning.
  • Mahadev B — UI/UX, testing, documentation and presentation.

ASTRAL is a preliminary exploration and planning prototype. Its terrain classifications and cost assumptions are provisional, and its generated routes are experimental rather than certified for operational rover navigation. Further scientific validation and testing would be required before real mission use.
